metadata.note: The South Pacific Coast Railroad, a 3 ft narrow-gauge steam railroad from the Alameda ferries to Santa Cruz via Newark, San Jose, Los Gatos and the Santa Cruz Mountains, with branches to Oakland (Webster Street) and Boulder Creek. Each section is drawn twice on identical geometry, per Rule 4: in SPC purple (#6B3FA0) to the July 1 1887 Southern Pacific lease, and in SP red (#C1272D) for the SP years, each section ending when its passenger service ended - San Leandro Bay crossing 1906, Alameda 1911 (electrified; the electric service belongs to SP's East Bay Electric Lines layer), Boulder Creek January 1934, the mountain line 1940, Los Gatos - San Jose January 1959, Newark - San Jose and Elmhurst - Newark May 1960. The mountain line is not drawn 1906-1909, when it was closed for earthquake repair and standard-gauge rebuilding.
metadata.source: OpenStreetMap relation 6773733 'South Pacific Coast Railroad' (ODbL) and OpenHistoricalMap relation 2749528 and Santa Cruz-area ways (CC0) for geometry - OHM dates were NOT used. Dates from Wikipedia 'South Pacific Coast Railroad', railswest.com SPC history, santacruztrains.com (Derek Whaley), the Alameda Post (Dennis Evanosky, citing Bruce MacGregor's 'South Pacific Coast'), Patch / Los Gatos Library, and Wikipedia 'Capitol Corridor'.
metadata.geometry_quality: Of 85.6 traced miles across 8 sections, 3.0 mi (the San Leandro Bay crossing, Alameda - Elmhurst) is a labelled straight line and 7.7 mi (Alameda's Main St / Central Ave / Encinal Ave, and Webster Street to Oakland) is street-routed on today's road grid; everything else follows OSM or OHM track. Alameda (north end of Main St) to Santa Cruz depot traces 75.9 mi against the documented 75.3 mi from the Alameda ferry slip (railswest). The mountain line is drawn on OHM's single, post-1909 standard-gauge alignment for the narrow-gauge years too (see the feature's geometry_quality). The San Jose approach is SP's 1935 alignment at Diridon. Despike / reversal / revisit checks run on every feature: a wye loop at Santa Cruz and a 200 m spur at Felton were removed.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: No SPC or SP timetable was consulted: every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh is an estimate except where a note quotes the 1887 counts (two daily Santa Cruz trains, four Boulder Creek locals). Open: the SPC/SP San Jose station alignment on The Alameda; the eastern landing of the San Leandro Bay bridge; when Webster Street steam trains became streetcars; whether local passenger trains ran Los Gatos - Wrights or Santa Cruz - Felton while the Summit tunnel was closed 1906-1909; whether the New Almaden branch (1886) carried passengers. Conflicts recorded in segment notes: Newark - San Jose completion 1876 vs 1877; Los Gatos opening June 1877 vs March 1878; Santa Cruz opening May 10 vs May 15 1880; last mountain train February 26 vs March 4 1940; last Los Gatos commute train 1955 (Wikipedia) vs January 23 1959 (Patch).
metadata.left_out: Not drawn: the Dumbarton Point - Newark ferry branch (1877-78 ferry connection; no surviving geometry, it would be a wholly ruled line); the Centerville branch (horse-worked 1881/82-1909, Rule 5); the New Almaden branch (1886; passenger service not established); the Dougherty Extension beyond Boulder Creek (logging); Olympia - Santa Cruz after 1940 (freight only, Rule 1); SP's East Bay Electric Lines, which used the Alameda SPC track from 1911 to 1941 (separate layer); Roaring Camp's Santa Cruz Big Trees & Pacific tourist trains on the Felton - Santa Cruz section (a different company, not part of this topic); and the Alameda Mole ferry pier.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Alameda Point – Fernside
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.
properties.geometry_quality: Street-routed approximation: no SPC track survives in Alameda. Drawn along today's Main Street, Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue on the OpenStreetMap road grid (5.3 mi), the streets the Alameda Post history names for the line, from the north end of Main Street (near the ferry terminal) to Encinal Avenue at Fernside Boulevard, where the San Leandro Bay bridge's western anchor stood. Not drawn: the 1884 'Alameda Mole', the ferry pier that ran about 2.5 mi out over the bay shallows west of Alameda Point. Block-level placement is not verified.

segments.note: Alameda end of the SPC main line, on Main Street, Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue. A test train ran on Encinal Avenue on December 2 1877 and service from Park Street to Los Gatos opened on March 20 1878; the line to the Alameda ferry slip was completed June 1 1878, and from July 1878 two ferries gave hourly Alameda - San Francisco sailings, which every SPC train met. The 'Alameda Mole' terminal opened March 15 1884. Southern Pacific leased the SPC from July 1 1887 (see the sp-spc- twin feature). headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: dates from railswest.com SPC history (March 20 / June 1 1878, March 15 1884, lease July 1 1887) and the Alameda Post history (route streets, December 2 1877 test run); hourly ferries from Wikipedia. Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Alameda – Elmhurst (San Leandro Bay bridge)
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.
properties.geometry_quality: STRAIGHT LINE, 3.0 mi, the whole feature: Encinal Avenue at Fernside Boulevard (Alameda, the bridge's documented western anchor) to the north end of the surviving UP Coast Subdivision at about 98th Avenue, Oakland (Elmhurst). The swing bridge across San Leandro Bay and the trestle-and-fill over the marsh are gone, and the eastern landing is not documented in any source consulted - the east end is an assumption that the line continued straight to the surviving ex-SPC track. Airport and Coliseum land now covers the route.

segments.note: The Bay and Coast Railroad, an SPC subsidiary, built the line north from Newark to Alameda on trestles and fill along the bay edge, crossing San Leandro Bay and its marsh on a swing bridge whose western anchor stood at today's Fernside Boulevard and Encinal Avenue. Opened with the Alameda line in March 1878. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 1878 opening from Wikipedia and railswest.com; bridge location from the Alameda Post history. Headway is an estimate.

properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.

The 1906-09 standard-gauge rebuild used the same corridor; no relocation is documented, but today's track may differ in detail from the 1878 narrow-gauge alignment.

segments.note: Bay and Coast Railroad line from Newark north along the eastern edge of the bay toward Alameda, opened March 1878 and run as the SPC main line between the Alameda ferries and San Jose / Santa Cruz. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 1878 completion from Wikipedia ('Bay and Coast Railroad completed a line of trestles and fill ... from Newark to Alameda') and railswest.com (March 20 1878). Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Newark – San Jose
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap relation 6773733: 16.6 mi, 13.9 mi on the UP Coast Subdivision (Newark - Alviso - Santa Clara) and 2.7 mi on the Caltrain Peninsula Subdivision into San Jose Diridon at The Alameda. LATER ALIGNMENT THAN THE ERA DRAWN at the San Jose end: the College Park - Diridon approach is Southern Pacific's 1935 consolidated route; the SPC's own narrow-gauge approach to its station on The Alameda was not traced and may differ by a few hundred metres.

segments.note: First section of the SPC, built from the Dumbarton Point ferry landing through Newark (company shops) and Alviso to San Jose, where the SPC had its station on The Alameda. Service between San Francisco (by the ferry Newark to Dumbarton Point) and the narrow gauge opened June 1 1877. SOURCE CONFLICT: Wikipedia says the line to San Jose was completed in 1876; railswest says construction reached San Jose by the end of 1877; 1877 is used because that is when the ferry connection - and so passenger service - began. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: June 1 1877 opening of ferry-and-train service from santacruztrains.com; Wikipedia and railswest.com give conflicting completion years (1876 vs end of 1877). Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: San Jose to Los Gatos via Campbell. SOURCE CONFLICT: santacruztrains.com says the track to Los Gatos was open by June 1 1877; Wikipedia gives 1878 and railswest.com says the Park Street (Alameda) - Los Gatos line opened March 20 1878. The later, two-source date is used. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: opening date from railswest.com (March 20 1878) and Wikipedia (1878); santacruztrains.com's June 1 1877 recorded as a conflict. Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Los Gatos – Santa Cruz
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenHistoricalMap ways (CC0, geometry only): relation 2749528 for Los Gatos - Zayante including the Wrights (Summit), Laurel and Mountain Charlie tunnels and the alignment now under Lexington Reservoir, then OHM 'Santa Cruz Big Trees & Pacific' and 'Santa Cruz & Felton Railroad' ways through Felton and the San Lorenzo gorge, plus 0.3 mi of OSM track into Santa Cruz depot. 24.7 mi. OHM's 1985 Rincon bypass and the pre-1879 Santa Cruz & Felton curve around Rincon were excluded, so the trace uses the 1879 Rincon (Coon Gulch) tunnel. ALIGNMENT CAVEAT: OHM records one alignment, i.e. the line as rebuilt to standard gauge in 1906-09. Tunnel #1 (Cats Canyon) was daylighted in 1903 and #7 (Hogsback) in 1898, and the Summit tunnel was re-bored after the 1906 earthquake shifted it 5 ft; no source consulted documents a relocation of the route, so the narrow-gauge era is drawn on this same line, which is not verified for the narrow-gauge years.

segments.note: Mountain line through eight tunnels, including the 6,200 ft Summit tunnel (Wrights - Laurel), joining the leased Santa Cruz and Felton Railroad near Felton for the run down the San Lorenzo gorge into Santa Cruz. Opened May 1880, 75.3 mi from the Alameda ferry slip. In 1887 two daily trains served Santa Cruz, plus excursion trains from the ferries to the mountain resorts. SOURCE CONFLICT on the opening day: santacruztrains.com says May 10 1880, railswest.com May 15 1880. headway_min 480 reflects the two daily trains and is approximate.
sources: Segment-level: opening May 1880 from santacruztrains.com (May 10) and railswest.com (May 15); 'two daily trains served Santa Cruz' from Wikipedia citing MacGregor.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Felton – Boulder Creek
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Narrow-gauge steam; no timetable was consulted for this figure.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenHistoricalMap ways (CC0, geometry only) for the Boulder Creek branch: 7.3 mi from the junction just south of Felton, across the San Lorenzo River, through Ben Lomond to Boulder Creek. The logging 'Dougherty Extension' beyond Boulder Creek is excluded.

segments.note: Felton and Pescadero Railroad, an SPC company incorporated June 13 1883, built from Felton up the San Lorenzo River through Pacific Mills (Ben Lomond) and reached Boulder Creek on April 26 1885. Wikipedia (citing MacGregor) says four daily locals served the branch; headway 240 is derived from that and is approximate.
sources: Segment-level: April 26 1885 arrival and 1883 incorporation from santacruztrains.com; 'four daily locals' from Wikipedia.

properties.line: South Pacific Coast: Alameda – Oakland (Webster Street)
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Street-running narrow-gauge steam local; no timetable was consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: Street-routed approximation (2.4 mi): Webster Street from Central Avenue in Alameda north through today's Webster Street/Posey tubes (the 1881 line used the municipal Webster Street bridge at the same place) to 12th and Webster, then on to 14th and Franklin, the 1886 terminus. The point where the Oakland line left the Alameda main line is assumed to be Central Avenue at Webster Street; no track survives.

segments.note: Oakland branch: from the Alameda line up Webster Street and across the municipal Webster Street bridge to a station at 12th and Webster, opened May 30 1881; extended to 14th and Franklin on October 1 1886. Railswest says SPC passengers beat Southern Pacific's San Francisco - Oakland commute time by eight minutes. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: May 30 1881 and October 1 1886 dates from railswest.com. Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: Southern Pacific: Alameda Point – Fernside (narrow gauge)
properties.geometry_quality: Street-routed approximation: no SPC track survives in Alameda. Drawn along today's Main Street, Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue on the OpenStreetMap road grid (5.3 mi), the streets the Alameda Post history names for the line, from the north end of Main Street (near the ferry terminal) to Encinal Avenue at Fernside Boulevard, where the San Leandro Bay bridge's western anchor stood. Not drawn: the 1884 'Alameda Mole', the ferry pier that ran about 2.5 mi out over the bay shallows west of Alameda Point. Block-level placement is not verified.

segments.note: Southern Pacific leased the South Pacific Coast from July 1 1887 (railswest.com) and ran its trains thereafter, so this era is drawn in SP colour as a separate feature on the same geometry (Rule 4). The Alameda Mole terminal burned November 20 1902 and was replaced; SP dual-gauged the line through Alameda in 1902 to add standard-gauge local trains. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: lease date, 1902 dual gauging from railswest.com; 1902 fire from the Alameda Post history. Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: The 1906 earthquake damaged the San Leandro Bay bridge, which was abandoned, isolating the Alameda track; Wikipedia says it 'could only be used for local service' thereafter. In 1911 SP electrified it as part of its East Bay Electric Lines (which ran here until January 1941) - that electric service is drawn in the East Bay electric layer, not here, so this feature ends at electrification. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 1906 isolation and 1911 electrification from Wikipedia and railswest.com. Headway is an estimate; the steam local service of 1906-1911 is described only in general terms by the sources.

properties.line: Southern Pacific: San Jose – Los Gatos
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenHistoricalMap relation 2749528 ways (CC0, geometry only; OHM dates not used) plus OSM relation 6773733 at Diridon and Vasona: 9.1 mi from The Alameda at Diridon to the site of Los Gatos station.

Narrow-gauge era; a third rail was laid into Los Gatos and the first standard-gauge freight arrived September 7 1895. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: lease date from railswest.com; 1895 third rail from santacruztrains.com (Los Gatos station). Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: Standard gauge; through trains to Santa Cruz resumed in 1909 and from 1927 the summer-Sunday Suntan Special excursions also ran this way to the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk. Los Gatos commute trains ran to San Jose and San Francisco. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: Suntan Special from 1927 per Wikipedia. Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: After the mountain line closed in 1940 the stub became SP's Los Gatos Branch, a commuter line. The last scheduled commute train left Los Gatos for San Jose at 7:59 p.m. on January 23 1959; the line was cut back to Vasona and later passenger service there came over the Los Altos Branch (not drawn here). SOURCE CONFLICT: Wikipedia says the last commuter train ran in 1955; the Los Gatos Library / Patch account of the January 1959 last train is followed. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: January 23 1959 last train from Patch (Los Gatos history column) and santacruztrains.com; Wikipedia's 1955 recorded as a conflict. Headway is an estimate.

properties.line: Southern Pacific: Los Gatos – Santa Cruz
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenHistoricalMap ways (CC0, geometry only): relation 2749528 for Los Gatos - Zayante including the Wrights (Summit), Laurel and Mountain Charlie tunnels and the alignment now under Lexington Reservoir, then OHM 'Santa Cruz Big Trees & Pacific' and 'Santa Cruz & Felton Railroad' ways through Felton and the San Lorenzo gorge, plus 0.3 mi of OSM track into Santa Cruz depot. 24.7 mi. OHM's 1985 Rincon bypass and the pre-1879 Santa Cruz & Felton curve around Rincon were excluded, so the trace uses the 1879 Rincon (Coon Gulch) tunnel. ALIGNMENT CAVEAT: OHM records one alignment, i.e. the line as rebuilt to standard gauge in 1906-09. Tunnel #1 (Cats Canyon) was daylighted in 1903 and #7 (Hogsback) in 1898, and the Summit tunnel was re-bored after the 1906 earthquake shifted it 5 ft; no source consulted documents a relocation of the route, so the narrow-gauge era is drawn on this same line, which is not verified for the narrow-gauge years.

segments.note: Southern Pacific leased the South Pacific Coast from July 1 1887 (railswest.com) and ran its trains thereafter, so this era is drawn in SP colour as a separate feature on the same geometry (Rule 4). Narrow gauge; an 1893 winter storm landslide forced major reconstruction. Ends April 1906: the earthquake shifted the Summit tunnel 5 ft and the line was rebuilt to standard gauge, reopening only in spring 1909 - so no through service is drawn 1906-1909 (local working at either end during the closure is not documented in the sources consulted). headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 1906 damage and 1909 reopening from Wikipedia and santacruztrains.com. Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: Reopened as standard gauge in spring 1909 (Summit tunnel work finished March 1909); reclassified a branch by 1915. From 1927 SP's Suntan Special summer excursions ran over it to the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk. Storm damage in February 1940 closed it; the line was formally abandoned in 1940. SOURCE CONFLICT on the last day: Wikipedia says the last train ran February 26 1940, railswest.com that passenger service ended March 4 1940; both fall in 1940. Olympia - Santa Cruz survived for freight (not drawn, Rule 1). headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 1909 reopening from santacruztrains.com and Wikipedia; 1940 end from Wikipedia (February 26) and railswest.com (March 4). Headway is an estimate.

segments.note: Southern Pacific leased the South Pacific Coast from July 1 1887 (railswest.com) and ran its trains thereafter, so this era is drawn in SP colour as a separate feature on the same geometry (Rule 4). The Felton and Pescadero line became SP's Felton, later Boulder Creek, Branch and carried passengers and freight until January 1934; in its last years service was by a McKeen motor car, and the branch was dismantled in 1934. When the branch was regauged is not documented in the sources consulted. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: Segment-level: 'remained in use as a passenger and freight line until January 1934' from santacruztrains.com (Felton & Pescadero); McKeen car and 1934 dismantling from Wikipedia. Headway is an estimate.

The point where the Oakland line left the Alameda main line is assumed to be Central Avenue at Webster Street; no track survives.

segments.note: Southern Pacific leased the South Pacific Coast from July 1 1887 (railswest.com) and ran its trains thereafter, so this era is drawn in SP colour as a separate feature on the same geometry (Rule 4). Railswest says the line through Oakland 'became a streetcar line, lasting through 1923'; when steam passenger trains gave way to streetcars is not documented in the sources consulted, so this feature stops at 1906, when the Alameda narrow-gauge system was cut off from the main line, and the later streetcar years are not drawn. headway_min is an estimate - no timetable was consulted for it.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1906 end year is a placeholder chosen to avoid claiming unverified service; only the lease date and the line's eventual conversion to a streetcar line (to 1923) are sourced.
